title: Perimeter control + k8s networkpolicies - terraform handoff
content:
Purpose
This is a working handoff doc for the infra team and platform SREs implementing perimeter controls and namespace-level network policy for Private (VPC/on-prem) deployments. Focus areas: private DNS resolution patterns, ingress/egress controls, central egress proxy options, firewall route rules, and Kubernetes NetworkPolicy/Cilium considerations.

High-level goals (non‑exhaustive)
- Enforce least-privilege egress from customer clusters while allowing managed platform services (metrics, package registries, telemetry).
- Keep internal private DNS authoritative within customer VPCs and forward external names safely.
- Provide Terraform modules that are re-usable between AWS and GCP private deployments with clear var surface.
- Provide rollback-safe upgrade steps and smoke tests for each change.

Assumptions / constraints
- Some customers run in air-gapped/offline sites; modules must support an optional "air_gapped=true" mode where external egress is completely blocked and operators can inject mirrors/caches.
- Customers want to avoid broad SNAT to internet; prefer an egress proxy (HTTP/HTTPS) with TLS interception avoided.
- Kubernetes clusters are Cilium-enabled in most installs but we must handle iptables-mode fallback for older clusters.
- Compliance requires audit logs for egress flows (at least metadata via proxy) and DNS queries (forwarder logging).

Design notes (short)
1) DNS: local authoritative + conditional forwarders
- Deploy a small DNS fleet inside the VPC (two Zonal placements, kept simple). Use CoreDNS with plugins: cache, forward, health, prometheus.
- CoreDNS config pattern: zone file for redwood-internal names (e.g., redwood.local) and conditional forwarding for external domains via an operator-configured outbound resolver pool.
- For split-horizon needs do NOT rely on Cloud DNS proxying; prefer a CoreDNS instance with explicit views if required.
- Terraform outputs: core_dns_security_group_id, core_dns_ips, core_dns_dns_name (for internal registrar).

2) Ingress pattern
- Ingress for customer apps: two-layer pattern. External traffic -> platform LB/edge -> service mesh ingress or L4 proxy. Keep DNS records in platform-managed private zone.
- For on-prem where a global load balancer is not available, provide a small HA pair of MetalLB + HAProxy configured by terraform module.

3) Egress approaches (pick one per customer)
- Option A: Egress proxy (preferred)
  - Envoy/HTTP proxy used for all HTTP/HTTPS egress.
  - Configure node-level transparent proxying via iptables TPROXY where supported, or set application env vars for platform-managed pods.
  - Proxy authenticates or mTLSs to the central egress service for audit/whitelisting.
- Option B: SNAT/NAT gateway (fallback)
  - Use a dedicated NAT gateway with restricted route table entries; avoid sharing NAT addresses across tenants in multi-tenant physical setups.

4) Firewall and route table guidance
- Small set of required egress ranges: update in terraform variable egress_well_known_services (list). Default must be empty to force explicit decisions.
- Route tables: keep separate route table for control-plane subnets, data-plane subnets, and dns-proxy subnets. Do not use a single default route for all private subnets unless explicitly approved.
- Security groups and firewall rules by intent (not IP): use tags/labels and explicit port ranges. Example rules:
  - Allow node -> core_dns_ips UDP:53, TCP:53
  - Allow nodes -> egress-proxy TCP:3128, 8443 (as configured)
  - Block outbound 0.0.0.0/0 except to egress-proxy or approved ranges (in non-air-gapped installs)
- Stateful firewall note: for on-prem we rely on customer edge firewalls. Document must include a checklist for firewall vendors (Palo Alto, FortiGate, Juniper).

5) Kubernetes NetworkPolicies (Cilium preferred)
- Default stance: deny-all ingress/egress at namespace level, then allow per-namespace exceptions via a standard allowlist module.
- Provide a terraform module to create the following policy templates (rendered as CRs):
  - platform-control-plane-allow (kube-system -> managed platform control plane endpoints)
  - infra-metrics-allow (namespaces labeled metrics=true -> allow egress to metrics destinations)
  - dns-egress-allow (allow pods to talk to core_dns_ips on 53)
  - egress-proxy-redirect (if using TPROXY, allow redirection ports)
- Cilium-specific notes: use ciliumfelix configuration to ensure host-reachable services are not accidentally blocked. Document a small helper script to validate the policy behavior using cilium policy trace.

Terraform module interface (proposed)
- Module: private_networking_core
  - vars (strings/lists): vpc_id, preferred_azs, subnet_map (map-string), env_tag, enable_egress_proxy (bool as string), egress_proxy_ips (list), core_dns_ami/image, air_gapped (bool as string), allowed_external_prefixes (list)
  - outputs (strings/lists): core_dns_ips, egress_proxy_ips, route_table_ids, control_plane_security_group_id
- Module: k8s_namespace_network_policies
  - vars: cluster_name, namespaces (list), default_deny (bool as string), dns_ips (list), egress_proxy_service (name), cilium_mode (bool as string)
  - outputs: policy_manifest_urls (list) — this is actually S3/GCS-hosted manifests location for ops to apply

Example var naming conventions (do this consistently)
- prefix all module vars with "infra_" where possible when used at root level to avoid collisions in large mono-repo terraform. E.g. infra_vpc_id, infra_env, infra_allowed_ecr_endpoints.

Upgrade/rollout plan (networking changes)
- Always start in canary VPC (small staging cluster)
- Steps for a typical upgrade that touches DNS or egress path:
  1) Open change ticket and pick a maintenance window. Notify impacted teams.
  2) Apply terraform in plan-only mode to canary, review diff.
  3) Deploy new CoreDNS or proxy in parallel (side-by-side) with new config (blue/green).
  4) Switch DNS clients to new IPs by updating route table or DNS resolver config.
  5) Run smoke tests: pod DNS resolution, external fetches via proxy, package manager downloads.
  6) Monitor telemetry for 30 minutes, rollback if >5% of requests fail vs baseline.
  7) Roll forward to remaining VPCs in waves.

Rollback steps (quick reference)
- If DNS regression: revert resolver IPs and flip back route table entries; confirm pod DNS lookup stability.
- If proxy causes failures: add an allowlist for specific domains or IPs, then revert traffic to previous NAT path.
- Have an emergency bypass: route table with explicit 0.0.0.0/0 to a known NAT gateway reserved for emergency use (lock behind approval).

Smoke tests (automation snippets to run after change)
- k8s: run from a busybox pod: nslookup api.redwood.internal -> expect core dns answer; curl https://package.registry.redwood.internal -> 200; curl https://example.com -> 200 via proxy (or blocked if air_gapped).
- tcpdump on node interface to confirm SNAT vs proxy port usage.
- Check CoreDNS metrics: cache_hits, forward_errors.

Operational playbook checklist (pre-deploy)
- Confirm maintenance window and ops on-call present.
- Backup current terraform state, snapshot route tables if provider supports it.
- Update runbook with new egress ranges and owner contacts.
- Make sure monitoring alerts for DNS/egress are actionable and have paging targets.

Unresolved questions / TODOs
- Decide default behavior for package managers (should we whitelist major registries by default?)
- Define standard naming convention for NAT IP pools vs egress-proxy IP pools in multi-tenant hosts.
- Should we bake in mutual TLS between proxy and central logging or leave to operator?

Notes to self (operator shorthand)
- When testing in GCP remember Cloud NAT preserves source ports differently than AWS NAT GW; test for 30k ephemeral port exhaustion in heavy egress scenarios.
- For on-prem installs, coordinate with customer firewall team to add short-lived allow rules rather than permanent wide opens.

References and quick links
- Basic cilium policy trace examples: https://cilium.io/docs/ (ops doc)
- CoreDNS recommended plugins: https://coredns.io/plugins/
- Example terraform pattern in infra repo: github.com/redwood-inference/infra/modules/private-networking (PR 487)

Appendix: quick snippet (example CoreDNS forward block)
- forward . 10.0.16.10 10.0.16.11 {
    policy sequential
    max_fails 2
    health_check 5s
  }

End.
